items.situation: I try to forget my ex and move on. But every day I wake up and see several things she bought me and I feel like a sledghammer hit me in the chest and stomach.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I tried to pack up the things Mara left here last night. Her mug's still by my bed.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Do you want me to come over now?

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Maybe. This morning I opened the closet and her coat was still over the chair. I'd forgotten it was there.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Okay. We can start with one drawer and stop.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I keep bringing a box into the room and leaving it in the doorway.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then I'll take the box when I get there.

items.thinking: The same concrete breakup-cleanup conversation can hold two attitudes: A may be slowly giving in to the work of clearing out reminders, or the reminders may be arriving as abrupt, alarming intrusions. A can make either sound after naming an object left behind, after discovering another object unexpectedly, and after describing the stalled attempt to pack. The slots all belong to A because the sounds are A's continuing reaction to the apartment and its contents; B's practical offers can answer either a subdued acceptance or a more urgent need for help.
items.reading_none: A is having difficulty sorting through belongings left by a former partner, and B offers to help. The words do not establish whether A is quietly working through it or being overwhelmed by the reminders.
items.reading_a: With sighs in every slot, A sounds resigned to the fact that the apartment still contains these things and to the slow, unfinished task of moving them out. B's offer becomes gentle companionship through a process A has not managed to finish alone.
items.why_a: Each sigh follows a factual encounter with an item or the stalled box. The low, accepting release turns the mug, coat, and doorway box into evidence of something A is reluctantly accommodating: the possessions remain for now, and the work will happen gradually. B's "one drawer and stop" and "when I get there" sound like permission to proceed at that pace.
items.reading_b: With screams in every slot, the objects and the act of packing become sudden, threatening triggers for A. B's offer reads as an attempt to get to A quickly and reduce the immediate exposure to the room and its contents.
items.why_b: Each scream can follow the unexpected sight of the mug, the rediscovered coat, or reaching the doorway with the box. The repeated abrupt reactions recast the same details as encounters that set off alarm rather than as items A is merely sad to leave behind. B's practical lines then sound like immediate containment: come over, limit the task, and remove the box.

turns.speaker: A

turns.speaker: B

Keeping all three slots with A makes the sounds a running stance toward the same account rather than isolated reactions.

items.reading_a: With a gasp after every A turn, the account becomes a chain of escalating, unexpected reversals: the route was longer than expected, the phone failed at the wrong moment, and then the elevator was improbably far away. A sounds caught off guard by each new development.
items.why_a: Each gasp can land as A relives the fresh realization in the preceding line: the unexpectedly long route, the phone dying just as it was needed, and the elevator being on twelve. B's questions then sound like they are drawing out an increasingly startling sequence.
items.reading_b: With a groan after every A turn, the same account becomes a sustained account of physical effort and mounting discomfort. The long route, searching for a place to go, and waiting outside the lobby all sound like stages of one drawn-out struggle.
items.why_b: Each groan can be an involuntary response to the effort described in the preceding line: continuing down the long loop, pressing on after the phone dies, and having to wait by the lobby doors. A sharp gasp and a scream both fit immediately after noticing the tapping and after spotting the figure/raised hand: in one reading the caller is startled by an unexplained visitor, in the other they perceive a threat. Keeping both slots with A makes the changing stance belong to the person seeing it, while B's questions stay practical and open.

items.reading_a: With gasps in both slots, A sounds repeatedly startled by a strange, unexpected nighttime visitor and by the unclear gesture. The call becomes a puzzled attempt to work out why someone is outside.
items.why_a: The gasp after the tapping makes the awakening feel abrupt and startling rather than immediately dangerous. The second gasp makes the raised hand another surprising detail, so B's question about what the person is pointing at sounds like a search for an explanation.
items.reading_b: With screams in both slots, A sounds as though the tapping and the figure by the gate are being experienced as an immediate threat. The call becomes B trying to assess a possible intrusion from limited information.
items.why_b: The scream after the first report frames the tapping as alarming rather than merely odd. The second scream turns the raised hand toward the glass into an escalation, so the later questions about the gesture, hedge, and light take on the meaning of checking what the person outside may do next.

items.why_a: After A reports the move date, a groan makes the proposed relocation sound physically and practically onerous rather than simply surprising. items.why_b: A scream after the offer makes the May start feel abruptly alarming.
